signals.title: NZD/JPY — G10 Bilateral Theme + BoJ Hike Speculation
signals.text: The G10 scorecard flags JPY as the weekly leader averaging +2.237% across 7 pairs, while NZD is the clear laggard averaging −1.464% across 4 pairs, producing a 3.701% spread. BoJ 1.0% holds a hike bias against RBNZ 2.75%, while New Zealand dollar positioning remains exceptionally stretched with COT leveraged funds net short −32,496 contracts at the 0th percentile of its 52-week range (z −2.60). JPY outperformance accelerates despite a nominal carry deficit, as domestic data beats reinforce BoJ tightening expectations ahead of the 18 September decision. Technical structure in NZD/USD shows price trading at 0.5883, pinned below its SMA20 of 0.5911, leaving cross downside exposed against broad JPY demand. Trade bias: Bearish NZD/JPY, driven by bilateral G10 momentum divergence and BoJ policy repricing. Catalyst: BoJ meeting 18 Sep. Risk: Leveraged funds cover crowded NZD short exposure, compressing the G10 performance spread below 1.20%.

signals.title: USD/JPY — Options Skew + Volatility Disconnect
signals.text: USD/JPY trades at 156.23, sitting firmly below its SMA20 of 159.04, SMA50 of 160.59, and SMA200 of 158.45. Saxo 25-delta risk reversals print at −2.64, signaling an extreme put skew as options participants aggressively price protection against base currency downside. Concurrently, ATM implied volatility sits at 7.2% against 30-day realized volatility of 10.1%, generating a negative volatility risk premium of −2.9%. This vol pricing reflects complacency in broader market pricing even as leveraged funds hold −81,619 net short contracts in JPY, vulnerable to rapid liquidation. Fed 3.75% vs BoJ 1.0% maintains a 267bp OIS carry advantage via SOFR-TONA, but policy tightening speculation continues to cap spot upside. Trade bias: Bearish USD/JPY, pressured by asymmetric downside options demand and moving-average breakdown. Catalyst: US NFP release today. Risk: Spot reclaims the SMA200 at 158.45, invalidating the technical breakdown.

signals.title: AUD/USD — Positioning + Retail Divergence
signals.text: AUD/USD trades at 0.7206, holding firmly above its SMA20 of 0.7129, SMA50 of 0.7035, and SMA200 of 0.6985. CFTC positioning shows institutional leveraged funds crowded long at +53,578 contracts, situated in the 95th percentile of its 52-week distribution with a z-score of +1.92. Conversely, Myfxbook retail sentiment registers 90% short, establishing an acute institutional versus retail positioning divergence at trend highs. RBA 4.35% vs Fed 3.75% provides a 70bp AUD carry premium via AONIA-SOFR differentials, while Australia inflation persistence keeps local policy restrictive. The combination indicates late-trend extension, where further gains threaten a forced capitulation of extreme retail short interest into resistance. Trade bias: Long AUD/USD, supported by carry advantage and retail short squeeze dynamics. Catalyst: RBA meeting 29 Sep. Risk: Spot closes below the SMA20 at 0.7129, signaling institutional long liquidation.

signals.title: EUR/USD — Macro Rates + Options Hedging Demand
signals.text: EUR/USD trades at 1.1624, positioned between its SMA20 of 1.1609 and its SMA200 of 1.1637. Fed 3.75% vs ECB 2.4% maintains a 135bp nominal carry spread in favor of the US dollar, reflected in a +146bp SOFR-€STR OIS advantage. Options markets display defensive characteristics, with implied volatility at 7.1% against a 30-day realized print of 4.7%, driving an elevated volatility risk premium of +2.5%. COT leveraged funds maintain net short exposure of −55,311 contracts at the 3rd percentile (z −2.28), though a weekly reduction of −55,635 contracts reflects rapid short-covering. Dovish remarks from Federal Reserve leadership have weakened the dollar index toward 99.08, yet overhead moving averages constrain topside momentum. Trade bias: Neutral EUR/USD, capped by structural USD carry advantage against technical resistance. Catalyst: ECB meeting 10 Sep. Risk: A daily close above the SMA200 at 1.1637, triggering extended institutional short covering.
